steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a conceptual, step-by-step walk-through of how a Transformer works. I’ve broken it into stages—encoder, decoder, and the core “attention” mechanism—so you can see how information flows and gets processed.

1. Input Representation  
   • Token Embedding  
     – Each input token (word piece, BPE, character, etc.) is mapped to a fixed-length vector via a lookup (“embedding”) table.  
   • Positional Encoding  
     – Because self-attention has no inherent notion of word order, we add (or concatenate) a position-dependent signal (sinusoidal vectors or learned embeddings).  
     – This lets the model distinguish “the cat sat on the mat” from “on the mat sat the cat.”

2. The Encoder Stack  
   A Transformer encoder is a stack of N identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers:
   a. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
      – Given the input vectors X = [x₁, x₂, …, xₙ], we compute three projections for each position:  
         • Queries Q = X·WQ  
         • Keys    K = X·WK  
         • Values  V = X·WV  
      – Attention scores: for each position i, we take the dot-product of Qi with all Kj to get scores.  
      – Softmax over scores → attention weights, then multiply those by V to get a context vector for position i.  
      – “Multi-head” means we do this in parallel with different WQ/WK/WV sets to capture different relationships.  
      – Result: each token’s representation is updated by a weighted sum of all other tokens’ representations.  
   b. Feed-Forward Network (FFN)  
      – A simple two-layer MLP applied independently to each position:  
         x → ReLU(x·W₁ + b₁) → (·W₂ + b₂)  
   c. Residual Connections and Layer Normalization  
      – We add the input of each sub-layer to its output (residual/“skip” connection), then apply layer norm.  
      – This helps training stability and gradient flow.

3. The Decoder Stack  
   Also a stack of N layers, but each layer has three sub-layers:
   a. Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention  
      – Same as encoder’s self-attention, but future positions are masked out (you can’t “look ahead” when generating).  
   b. Encoder–Decoder Attention  
      – Queries come from the previous decoder sub-layer; Keys and Values come from the top of the encoder stack.  
      – This lets the decoder focus on relevant parts of the input.  
   c. Feed-Forward Network + Residual + Layer Norm (same as in encoder).

4. Final Linear + Softmax  
   • The decoder’s final output vectors are projected into the vocabulary space (via a linear layer) and then passed through a softmax to produce a probability distribution over next tokens.  
   • During training, you compare this distribution to the ground-truth next token and compute cross-entropy loss.

5. Why Attention?  
   – Traditional RNNs process sequentially; Transformers process all positions in parallel.  
   – Self-attention lets every token “attend” to every other token directly, making it easy to capture long-range dependencies.  
   – Multi-head attention allows the model to pick up different kinds of relationships at once (syntax, semantics, coreference, etc.).

6. Training and Inference  
   • Training  
     – You feed the entire input (and, for teacher-forced decoder, the previous correct outputs) simultaneously, compute loss, and backpropagate.  
   • Inference (autoregressive generation)  
     – You generate one token at a time: feed in the already-generated tokens, compute probabilities, pick the next token, append it, repeat (often with beam search or sampling).

Key Takeaways  
– A Transformer’s power comes from self-attention: a flexible, parallelizable way to mix information across positions.  
– Stacking layers, using multiple heads, and adding residual connections lets the model learn very rich representations.  
– Separating encoder and decoder (with cross-attention) makes it ideal for sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation, summarization, and dialogue.
